newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan monopoly eyes Iraq oil in wider cooperation.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan monopoly eyes Iraq oil in wider cooperation.

text.p: Taiwan monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp would consider buying Iraqi crude if a deal were linked to wider cooperation, but no longer sees urgency to join a U.N.-brokered oil-for-food plan, executives said on Tuesday.

"We usually want to negotiate oil purchase deals with other countries that are tied to cooperation plans like oil exploration and drilling agreements," Chinese Petroleum vice president Chang Hung-chiang told Reuters by telephone.
"Our oil supply has no shortages now, so there is no urgency to buy Iraqi crude," Chang said.
After months of political delays, Iraq won the right on Tuesday to sell limited amounts of crude to finance imports of food and humanitarian aid under a U.N.-brokered deal.
Chinese Petroleum had contacted Iraq's state oil company as early as June to explore purchases under the oil-for-food scheme as well as possible cooperation in oil extraction.
The contacts, politically controversial at the time due to problems with the United Nations plan and Taiwan's estrangement from the world body, had received few "positive responses," Chang said.

Company spokesman Fang Yi-shan told Reuters in September that Taiwan no longer sought Iraqi crude under the U.N. scheme, and blamed possible interference by China -- a U.N. security council member that regards Taiwan as a renegade province.

Beijing took China seat in the U.N. from Taipei in 1971 when the island's exiled Republic of China government was expelled from the world body. The republican government fled to Taiwan after its civil war defeat to the communists in 1949.
Beijing works actively to isolate Taiwan diplomatically, pushing to gain sovereignty over the Nationalist-ruled island.
"We know that China would not let Taiwan get Iraq's oil through the U.N., so Chinese Petroleum quit considering the oil-for-food programme," Fang said on September 4.
Iraq nevertheless remained on Chinese Petroleum's list of potential oil suppliers, Fang said at the time.
Chang confirmed that policy toward Iraq had not changed and that Taiwan was willing to buy from Iraq's state oil company if this were possible.
Crude purchases should be a simple business matter between Chinese Petroleum and an overseas supplier with no need for U.N. involvement, Chang added.

Taiwan and its powerful export-driven economy are highly dependent on imported crude for domestic energy, buying some 150 million barrels a year. Nuclear power provides only about 10 percent of local consumption.
